divisions.question: Lin Thorp As an educationalist, I find it disturbing that this place is being used to consider quite a retrograde step in educational history. There is a movement in education that has been going on since the late eighties, with a move from prescriptive assessment to descriptive assessment, and from time based learning to competency based learning. It is recognising what learning is. It is recognising that individuals learn at different paces and in different methods to come to the same place, which is a level of competency in a particular area. Time based learning is going back to the past. Time based learning presumes that you have a group of students—whether they be young school students or people who are studying, in this case, to be engineers—who are all in the same room, at the same time, with the same teacher, and, at the end of that particular period of time, they are all qualified to do a particular task. That is not the way education works today. Education works today on the acquiring of skills. It does not matter whether it be about learning how to be a barista or how to be a neurosurgeon. I, for one, would prefer, if I were to be under the knife in a serious operation, to know that that particular individual had not just served time at university for a number of years but had reached the level of competency that they deserve. This is what this is all about. Going along with the analogy of medical training, in a different job I worked for the medical school of Tasmania. My task was to review the curriculum of the six-year course for all students doing a Bachelor of Medicine and a Bachelor of Medical Science. What became very clear during that exercise was that so much of that training was time based and it needed to move. Over the years, more and more had been added to the curriculum, based simply on facts and figures, rote learning, if you like, and it needed in to be brought up to the end of the 20th century, as it was then—this was back in the 1990s. speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: Introduced the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013 to restore maritime safety training standards weakened by the 2012 national shipping law, opposing a proposal to cut the required training period for engineer watchkeepers from 36 months to just 12 months.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: Introduced the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill to reverse a reduction in training standards caused by the Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law, noting a 2009 agreement between engineers and the safety regulator to enhance qualifications has stalled, and proposed codifying minimum training time after learning the regulator wanted to cut onboard training by two-thirds.

speeches.speaker: Chris Bowen
speeches.brief: Addressed the bill, explaining concern stems from international changes to seafarer training standards that reduced the minimum requirement from three years to 12 months, reportedly instigated by Iran, and noted the Australian Maritime Safety Authority gave sworn evidence to a Senate estimates hearing on 23 May 2012 that it had no intention of adopting the reduced standard.

speeches.speaker: Warren Truss
speeches.brief: Addressed the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill, noting the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers represents around 3,000 marine engineers who raised concerns that a proposed review of Marine Orders Part 3 would water down qualification standards, and said the regulator has since withdrawn its draft order for further consultation, with only four weeks of parliamentary sittings remaining before the election.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Argued that the minority parliament had delivered measures including $13 billion for clean and renewable energy, a tax-free threshold of $18,200, dental treatment from 1 January 2014, and stronger firefighter protections. Supported the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013, defending minimum standards and calling for protections for marine engineers and a safe Australian-owned shipping industry.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: Summed up the dispute behind the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill, centred on a proposal to cut required training from three years to one and abolish a mandatory verbal competency test, noting the union had agreed in principle to some reforms while the minister warned the bill would leave Australia with outdated standards inconsistent with global shipping conventions, before the debate was interrupted.

speeches.speaker: Joel Fitzgibbon
speeches.brief: Raised concerns about the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill on National TAFE Day, warning proposed changes could cut required marine engineer training from three years to one year, and urged the minister and the Australian Maritime Safety Authority to renegotiate with the Australian Institute of Marine Engineers to protect shipping safety standards.

speeches.speaker: Robert McClelland
speeches.brief: Supported the Marine Engineers Qualifications Bill 2013, arguing it would prevent Australian marine and power engineering standards from being reduced to lower international standards and would protect vessel, environmental, crew and national security interests.
